Linear Mixed Models in Jamovi

A step-by-step walkthrough using attractiveness rating data

The Jamovi interface

Before running anything, it helps to know what you're looking at. The Linear Mixed Model analysis in Jamovi has three main panels — the variable assignment screen, the fixed effects panel, and the random effects panel. We'll use all three.

Panel 1 — Variable assignment

This is the first screen you see when you open the analysis. The variable list on the left shows every column in your dataset. You drag or arrow variables into the appropriate boxes in the middle, and results update live in the pane on the right.

The four boxes in the middle each have a specific role:

BoxWhat goes in itIn our study
Dependent Variable The outcome you want to model — must be continuous attr (attractiveness rating)
Factors Categorical predictors (nominal variables) cosmetics (0 = no makeup, 1 = makeup)
Covariates Continuous predictors ICS (added later for H4 onwards)
Cluster variables The grouping variables that define your random effects — who or what observations are nested within pid and faceid
Cluster variables vs. random effects: putting a variable in the Cluster box just tells Jamovi it exists as a grouping factor. What you actually do with it — intercept only, intercept plus slope — is set separately in the Random Effects panel below.

The right-hand pane shows results as soon as the model runs. You'll see sections for Model Fit, Fixed Effects, Parameter Estimates, and Random Components — we'll refer to each of these as we go through the hypotheses.

Panel 2 — Fixed Effects

Fixed effects are the main predictors whose coefficients you want to estimate and interpret — the things you'd put in a standard regression. They appear in the Parameter Estimates table on the right.

The Components box on the left lists any variables you've added as Factors or Covariates. Use the arrow buttons to move them into Model Terms on the right. The two arrow buttons do slightly different things:

ButtonWhat it does
→ (plain arrow) Adds the selected variable as a main effect
→▾ (arrow with dropdown) Lets you add an interaction term between two or more selected variables

The Intercept checkbox at the bottom is ticked by default — leave it on. For H1–H3 the only model term you need is cosmetics. We add ICS and the interaction from H4 onwards.

Panel 3 — Random Effects

This is the panel that makes it a mixed model. Random effects allow the model to estimate how much the relationship varies across your grouping units — participants, faces, schools, items, and so on.

The workflow here is: drag a term from Components into Random Coefficients. Each term you add becomes a random effect for whichever cluster variable is currently selected.

The options at the bottom are worth knowing:

OptionWhat it means
Effects correlation → Correlated The intercept and any slopes are allowed to correlate with each other (default, and usually the right choice)
Effects correlation → Not correlated Forces intercepts and slopes to be independent — a simpler model, sometimes needed if the full model won't converge
LRT for Random effects Runs a likelihood ratio test to ask whether each random effect significantly improves fit — useful for comparing models
Random coefficients Shows the estimated random effect for every individual unit (every participant, every face) — the BLUPs
The core idea: a fixed effect says "on average, across everyone, cosmetics increases attractiveness by X." A random effect says "but that average masks real variation — some participants show a bigger effect, some smaller, and the model estimates that spread." Both matter.

Setup & Data

The study

45 participants each rated a subset of 70 faces, seen both with and without cosmetics, on attractiveness (1–7). Each participant also completed the Intrasexual Competitiveness Scale (ICS). The dataset is in long format — one row per participant–face combination.

VariableTypeDescription
pidID / NominalParticipant identifier
faceidID / NominalFace stimulus identifier
cosmeticsNominal (0/1)0 = no makeup, 1 = makeup
ICSContinuousIntrasexual Competitiveness Scale score (z-scored)
attrContinuousAttractiveness rating (1–7, outcome variable)

Loading the data

  1. Open Jamovi. Go to ☰ → Open → Browse and select low_n_missing.csv.
  2. Check that the data has loaded correctly — you should see 3,669 rows and 5 columns.
  3. Set variable types: pid and faceid → ID; cosmetics → Nominal; ICS and attr → Continuous.

Installing the gamlj module

Mixed models in Jamovi are handled by the gamlj (General Analyses for Linear Models in Jamovi) module.

  1. Click Modules (top-right) → Jamovi library.
  2. Search for gamlj and install it.
  3. Once installed, mixed models appear under Linear Models → Mixed Model.
Note: All five models below use the same outcome variable (attr) and build progressively. You can re-open the same analysis and add complexity rather than starting fresh each time.
H1 Do cosmetics increase attractiveness?

The traditional approach requires averaging all ratings for each participant (or each face) before running a paired t-test. This throws away data and forces a choice — by participant or by face — that changes your power and what you can test.

A mixed model uses every row, avoids aggregation, and simultaneously accounts for both sources of clustering.

Traditionally, you'd have to average across one grouping before you could even start. That forces a choice — and the choice changes your results.

ApproachModelProblem
By face attr ~ cosmetics + (1|faceid) Loses all participant information; can't test ICS
By participant attr ~ cosmetics + (1|pid) Loses all face information; fewer observations
All at once attr ~ cosmetics + (1|pid) + (1|faceid) Uses all 3,669 rows; accounts for both clusterings

We run all three so you can see what changes — then use the "all at once" model going forward.

Jamovi steps — Model 1: By face

  1. Go to Analyses → Linear Models → Mixed Model.
  2. Move attr into Dependent Variable.
  3. Move cosmetics into Covariates.
  4. Move faceid into Cluster variables.
  1. Open the Fixed Effects panel — move cosmetics into Model Terms.
  2. Open the Random Effects panel — you should see Intercept | faceid and cosmetics | faceid in Components. Move Intercept | faceid into Random Coefficients.
  3. Run.

Model 1 output

What to look for

  1. Compare the cosmetics estimate and CI across all three models. The "all at once" version should have the narrowest confidence interval — it loses no data to aggregation.
  2. Variance components (Model 3): three rows — pid, faceid, Residual — showing how variance is partitioned across sources.

Cosmetics effect across all three models

ModelEstimateSE95% CI Lower95% CI UpperCI width
By face  (1|faceid)0.3870.0470.2950.4790.184
By participant  (1|pid)0.3840.0490.2890.4800.191
All at once  (1|pid) + (1|faceid)0.3750.0420.2920.4570.165

The estimates are nearly identical across models, but the "all at once" model has the narrowest confidence interval — it uses all the data with no aggregation, so it is most certain about the effect.

Key point: The "all at once" model wins on every dimension — more data used, no arbitrary aggregation choice, and it directly estimates how much of the variance comes from faces vs. participants vs. everything else.

H2 Is the effect of makeup the same for all observers?

H1 estimated a single makeup effect — the same for every participant. But people may differ: some observers might be strongly influenced by makeup, others barely at all. We can let that effect vary across participants by adding a random slope for cosmetics within pid.

attr ~ cosmetics + (1 + cosmetics | pid) + (1 | faceid)

The only change from H1 is highlighted in yellow above: the pid random effect now includes a slope for cosmetics, not just an intercept.

Jamovi steps

  1. Starting from the H1 "all at once" model, keep all settings as they are.
  2. In the Random Effects panel, move cosmetics | pid into Random Coefficients alongside the two intercepts already there.
  3. Run.

Random Coefficients now contains three terms: Intercept | pid, Intercept | faceid, and cosmetics | pid. The model will estimate how much the makeup effect varies across participants.

H2 output

Model: attr ~ 1 + cosmetics + (1 + cosmetics | pid) + (1 | faceid)  ·  N = 3,669  ·  Converged: yes

Random Parameters Correlations

GroupParameter 1Parameter 2Correlation
pidInterceptcosmetics slope0.878
Key point: The cosmetics SE has widened from ~0.04 to 0.158 — the model is now honest that the effect varies a lot across participants (SD = 1.017). The high positive correlation (0.878) tells us that participants who rate faces higher overall also tend to show a bigger boost from cosmetics.
Worth pausing on: the SD of the cosmetics slope across participants is 1.017 — larger than the average effect itself (0.404). That means the variation in how much observers respond to makeup is greater than the average makeup effect. Some participants show a large boost, others show none, and some may even show a negative effect. A single fixed effect would completely hide this.
Key point: If the SD of the cosmetics slope across participants is large relative to the fixed effect, observers vary substantially in how they respond to makeup. The correlation between intercept and slope tells you whether stricter raters show a smaller (or larger) makeup boost.
Shrinkage: Participants with fewer ratings will have their estimated slopes "pulled" towards the group average — this is deliberate. The model is more conservative for those we have less data on.
↑ Back to top
H3 Is the effect of makeup the same for all faces?

Just as observers can differ in how they respond to makeup, faces can differ in how much makeup changes their perceived attractiveness. Some faces may benefit greatly from cosmetics; others might not at all. This is impossible to test cleanly with traditional approaches — a separate regression per face is not viable because each face only has two "versions" (makeup / no makeup).

We simply add a random slope for cosmetics within faceid.

attr ~ cosmetics + (1 + cosmetics | pid) + (1 + cosmetics | faceid)

The only change from H2: the faceid block now also gets a cosmetics slope.

Jamovi steps

  1. Starting from the H2 model, go to the Random Effects panel.
  2. Move cosmetics | faceid into Random Coefficients — it now contains all four terms: Intercept | pid, Intercept | faceid, cosmetics | pid, and cosmetics | faceid.
  3. Run.

H3 output

Model: attr ~ 1 + cosmetics + (1 + cosmetics | pid) + (1 + cosmetics | faceid)  ·  N = 3,669  ·  Converged: yes

Key point: Faces vary substantially in how much makeup helps them — the SD of the faceid cosmetics slope is 0.731. Combined with the pid slope SD of 1.024 from H2, both sources of variation are real and large. The correlations (~0.88 for both) tell a consistent story: more attractive faces and more generous raters both show a bigger makeup boost.

A free gift

By fitting this model to answer H2 and H3, we automatically get something extra — without any additional work. The model estimates both an intercept and a slope for every observer and every face:

Random effectWhat it captures
Intercept (pid / faceid)How much higher or lower that person/face scores on average — baseline attractiveness or rater generosity
Slope for cosmetics (pid / faceid)How much that person/face responds to cosmetics — their individual makeup boost

And because the model estimates both simultaneously, it also gives us the correlation between them — for free. In our data:

GroupCorrelationInterpretation
Observers (pid)0.876More generous raters also show a bigger makeup boost
Faces (faceid)0.880More attractive faces benefit more from cosmetics
Why this matters: these correlations are substantive findings in their own right — not just model diagnostics. You get them simply by fitting the model correctly. A traditional aggregated approach would never surface them.
Key point: The model now estimates how much of the variance in the makeup effect is attributable to differences between observers vs. differences between faces — a distinction that is lost the moment you aggregate.
↑ Back to top
H4 Does the makeup effect depend on observer ICS?

ICS (intrasexual competitiveness) is a continuous participant-level score. We want to know whether observers who score higher on ICS show a different response to makeup. This is an interaction between a face-level variable (cosmetics) and a person-level continuous variable (ICS).

Traditional approaches require chopping ICS into groups (e.g., median split or tertiles) and using a mixed-design ANOVA. The problem: the interaction result changes depending on how you cut, and cutting a continuous variable loses information and statistical power.

attr ~ cosmetics + ICS + cosmetics:ICS + (1 + cosmetics | pid) + (1 + cosmetics | faceid)

Jamovi steps

  1. Starting from the H3 model, move ICS into Covariates alongside cosmetics.
  2. Keep pid and faceid in Cluster variables as before.
  1. In the Fixed Effects panel, both cosmetics and ICS appear in Components. Select both and use the →▾ button to add the interaction term — you should see cosmetics, ICS, and cosmetics ✻ ICS in Model Terms.
  2. Random Effects stay exactly as in H3: Intercept | pid, Intercept | faceid, cosmetics | pid, cosmetics | faceid.
  3. Run.

H4 output

Model: attr ~ 1 + cosmetics + ICS + cosmetics:ICS + (1 + cosmetics | pid) + (1 + cosmetics | faceid)  ·  N = 3,669  ·  Converged: yes

Key point: ICS alone is not significant (p = .438), but the interaction with cosmetics is (p = .027). The negative coefficient (-0.392) means that as ICS increases, the makeup boost decreases — highly competitive observers show a smaller response to cosmetics. This is exactly what could not be tested cleanly with a median split or tertile approach.

Unpacking the interaction — Estimated Marginal Means

Once we have evidence of an interaction, we probe it using Estimated Marginal Means (EMM). The idea is to pin ICS at meaningful values (low, medium, high = −1 SD, mean, +1 SD) and estimate the predicted attractiveness rating at each combination of cosmetics and ICS level.

  1. Go to the Estimated Marginal Means section in gamlj.
  2. Add a term with both cosmetics and ICS.
  3. Jamovi automatically pins ICS at Mean−1SD, Mean, and Mean+1SD.
  4. Run — three tables appear: marginals for cosmetics, for ICS, and for the interaction.

The most informative table is the interaction — it shows predicted attractiveness at each combination of cosmetics level and ICS level:

Cosmetics (no makeup)ICS levelMeanSE95% CI
No makeupLow (−1 SD)3.470.089[3.29, 3.65]
No makeupMean3.570.074[3.42, 3.72]
No makeupHigh (+1 SD)3.670.091[3.49, 3.85]
MakeupLow (−1 SD)3.850.160[3.53, 4.16]
MakeupMean3.770.129[3.51, 4.03]
MakeupHigh (+1 SD)3.690.164[3.37, 4.02]
Reading the interaction: at low ICS, makeup raises the mean from 3.47 to 3.85 — a clear boost. At high ICS, the gap almost disappears (3.67 vs 3.69). Highly competitive observers barely respond to cosmetics at all. The interaction is doing real work here, not just statistical noise.

Pairwise contrasts — where does the makeup effect hold?

We can directly test the makeup vs no-makeup difference at each ICS level. Jamovi's EMM pairwise comparison output gives us:

ICS levelContrast (makeup − no makeup)SEtp
Low (−1 SD)1.1590.2564.52<.001
Mean0.7670.1744.40<.001
High (+1 SD)0.3760.2321.62.106
The punchline: the makeup effect is statistically clear at low and average ICS, but disappears entirely for highly competitive observers. This is the kind of nuanced conclusion that would be lost the moment you forced ICS into categories.
Key point: The makeup effect is significant at low and medium ICS but not at high ICS — meaning highly competitive observers show a smaller (potentially non-existent) boost from cosmetics. Using a continuous moderator without arbitrary cuts gives a single, stable p-value and a richer story.

H5 Do faces differ in how much they are affected by observer ICS?

So far, the effect of ICS on attractiveness ratings has been treated as fixed — the same across all faces. But that assumption can be relaxed. Some faces might attract harsher ratings from competitive observers; others might not. We add ICS as a random slope within faceid.

There is no straightforward way to test this outside of an LMM.

attr ~ cosmetics + ICS + cosmetics:ICS + (1 + cosmetics | pid) + (1 + cosmetics + ICS | faceid)

Jamovi steps

  1. Starting from the H4 model, keep all fixed effects unchanged.
  2. In the Random Effects panel, move ICS | faceid into Random Coefficients — it now sits alongside Intercept | pid, Intercept | faceid, cosmetics | pid, and cosmetics | faceid.
  3. Run.

H4 vs H5 — what changes when we add the ICS random slope?

Adding the ICS random slope for faceid changes the uncertainty around the ICS fixed effect:

TermH4 EstimateH4 SEH4 pH5 EstimateH5 SEH5 p
cosmetics0.3960.174.0260.4040.175.024
ICS-0.0840.107.438-0.0980.122.428
cosmetics ✻ ICS-0.3920.171.027-0.4170.172.020
Worth noting: the ICS SE widens from 0.107 to 0.122 once we allow the ICS effect to vary across faces. H4 was underestimating the uncertainty — it assumed the ICS effect was the same for every face, which it isn't. H5 gives a more honest picture.
Key point: Ignoring that the ICS effect varies across faces makes its uncertainty look smaller than it really is. The H5 model gives a more realistic picture — and the shift in the ICS p-value (from ~.05 in H4 to non-significant in H5) illustrates why model structure matters for inference.

Model build-up — quick reference

Each hypothesis adds one step to the model. The table below shows the full progression.

Hypothesis Model formula New element
H1 attr ~ cosmetics + (1|pid) + (1|faceid) Random intercepts for participants and faces
H2 + (1+cosmetics|pid) Cosmetics slope varies by participant
H3 + (1+cosmetics|faceid) Cosmetics slope varies by face
H4 + ICS + cosmetics:ICS Continuous moderator (ICS) + interaction
H5 + (1+cosmetics+ICS|faceid) ICS slope varies by face
Convergence: More complex random effects structures sometimes fail to converge, especially with small N or sparse data. If Jamovi reports a convergence warning, try simplifying: remove the intercept–slope correlation (use || syntax if available) or drop the most complex random slope first.
